To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the kidney plays an important role in the handling and degradation of insulin in the body.
insulin is reabsorbcd by renal tubular epithelial cells by a process that is mediated by a low-affinity, insulin-specific binding site on the luminal brush-border membrane.
insulin is reabsorption in the renal tubular epithelial cell by binding to the cell surface, followed by endocytosis and degradation of the hormone in lysosomal vacuoles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which insulin is handled by the kidney.
the mechanism of renal tubular reabsorption of filtered insulin in the kidney, a mechanism which is of considerable importance to the overall homeostatic control of circulating insulin levels.
the mechanism of renal insulin handling and has focused on the role of the kidney in the disposal of insulin in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
insulin binds to renal BBM with a high capacity but a low affinity and that this binding is followed by the degradation of insulin to TCA-soluble fragments.

insulin binding to renal brush border membranes is mediated by low-affinity, low-capacity sites which are distinct from the biological receptors and which can be readily differentiated from the insulin-like-growth factors and other low-molecular weight proteins.

insulin binding and degradation by brush border membranes is a saturable process which is not inhibited by insulin analogues, IGF-I or IGF-II, but which is inhibited by insulin, proinsulin, and desoctapeptide insulin.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding and degradation of insulin by renal brush border membrane is not due to the high-affinity insulin-receptor but to low-affinity, insulin-specific sites.
insulin reabsorption in the kidney is mediated by low-affinity, low-capacity binding sites on the brush border membrane of the renal tubule.

we have identified a low affinity, high-capacity insulin recognition system on the luminal surface of the proximal tubular brush border membrane which is capable of distinguishing insulin from the insulin-related growth factors and other polypeptides and proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the kidney plays a major, but previously unrecognized role in insulin homeostasis.
insulin is taken up into the renal tubule by the same mechanism by which it is taken up in the intestinal mucosa.
there are low-affinity, low-capacity, insulin receptors in renal brush border membranes that are distinct from insulin receptors in renal cells.
